prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place B020 first, and my own view has not moved. The chain runs from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, to the biology of GLP-1 and GLP-2 and then to durable receptor agonists. It is original, mechanistically complete and independently confirmed, and it has produced large randomized outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. As a physician-scientist I weigh the combination of a clean discovery chain and a measurable change in patient outcomes heavily, and few candidates match it. The three-person academic configuration of Holst (physiology), Mojsov (active peptide) and Drucker (biology and translational pharmacology) gives each discovery step a distinct, defensible owner.
statement.case_against: The credit is not clean. Habener and others contributed to identifying the active peptide, and the Mojsov priority question is genuinely contested. Leaving out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues are what actually reached patients, can be criticised as honouring the discovery and ignoring the drug that delivered it. Long-term safety and durability of the obesity indication are still being defined. Finally, unanimous opening support is not a measure of merit. We should test the attribution as hard as we test the science.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the design of liraglutide and semaglutide is what turned the physiology into a therapy, and that Mojsov's role is more arguable.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's work is what reached patients, and I would not call it minor. But the prize is for discovery, and Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a discovery-level step that the drug programmes depended on. The disputed priority between Mojsov and Habener is a reason to examine the evidence, not to replace her with an industrial contribution. I would keep Knudsen in the citation text only if the committee prefers a physiology-plus-translation framing, and then I would drop the contested name rather than the physiologist. I remain with the three academic discoverers.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked CAR-T second with June and Sadelain only, doubting that Rosenberg's contribution to CAR design is decisive, and ranked BCR-ABL inhibition third.
responses.response: I agree that Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a different achievement from receptor engineering, and that a June and Sadelain pairing is more defensible than the supplied trio. My reservation is that Eshhar's original chimeric-receptor concept is outside the credited names, so a clean CAR-T allocation is not available from this list. That is why I rank B040 below TNF blockade, where the attribution is cleaner, although I accept that the CAR-T patient impact is striking.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked the unfolded protein response second for Mori and Walter, citing a mechanistically complete, conserved pathway with a clean two-person attribution, and he placed chaperonin folding third.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual strength of UPR, and the Mori and Walter attribution is clean. My disagreement is about weighting. Its medical consequence is still indirect and therapeutic efforts have not yet delivered an approved drug, whereas B020 and the TNF candidate (B034) show benefit to patients. I would not rule UPR out, but I would hold it for later and not put it ahead of candidates with demonstrated outcomes.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, noted that Knudsen is left out only because of the three-name limit and that delaying the incretin prize risks mis-allocation as the field expands, and he placed optogenetics third with a Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann split.
responses.response: I agree that timing matters and that B020 should not wait. On optogenetics I am more cautious than he is. With six credited names, any three-person split leaves out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, and direct patient benefit is still early, so I would rank it below the immunology and oncology candidates until the attribution question is resolved.

responses.point: El Manira placed optogenetics second and noted that GLP-1 attribution is plausible for Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, with Habener not on the list and industry developers outside the discovery frame.
responses.response: I agree on the GLP-1 trio. On optogenetics I accept that it is a major and widely used method, but our common criteria call for discovery and a lasting benefit to the prize's purpose, and a tool with limited clinical translation and an unresolved six-way credit should not displace a candidate with proven patient benefit. If the committee wants a method prize, the allocation needs to be settled first.

uncertainties: Whether the Habener contribution and the Mojsov priority question can be resolved from the evidence, and whether it changes the three names.
Whether the committee should credit the pharmaceutical developer (Knudsen) alongside or instead of a discoverer.
Whether a second part is feasible given that B020 already uses three names, since a two-part prize would force fewer names on the GLP-1 part.
My fallback ordering (B034, then B040) depends on attribution issues I cannot fully resolve from the supplied credit, including TNF cloning and antibody engineering and Eshhar's CAR concept.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B020. B034 (TNF blockade in rheumatoid arthritis) lies in my own field of experimental rheumatology, which I flag for transparency. My profile documents no co-authorship or institutional tie to Feldmann or Maini, so I see no recusal basis, but the committee may wish to note the field proximity.
